## TL;DR

Added pull-down refresh to the Hub server picker. A downward pull beginning at the top of the saved-server list asks the app to run its existing reachability refresh, and a compact spinning arrow remains visible until that full asynchronous check settles. Added tests for the request, indicator, and row-menu exclusion. The Android Hub guide does not describe a refresh interaction, so it needed no edit.

## Work and rationale

The server list component already owns list scrolling and long-press row reordering, while the reachability requests live in `mobile/src/app-state.ts`. Keeping network work in app state and letting the component emit a `refresh` event preserves that division. `App.vue` imports the existing `refreshReachability()` function and wraps it with a `refreshingReachability` flag. The flag is set before the request starts and cleared in `finally`, so the indicator also clears if the promise rejects. Repeated requests are ignored while one is in flight. Since `refreshReachability()` uses `Promise.all` around the server checks, this duration includes each server's result or its validation timeout.

The list tracks a single touch only when its scroll position is at the top and the gesture did not start on a row's edit menu. Downward travel is damped for the pull distance and triggers one refresh at the threshold; upward motion, multi-touch, drags, and menu-origin gestures do not request a refresh. The touch move is canceled while the pull is active to prevent the view from scrolling away from the gesture. `overscroll-behavior-y: contain` limits browser-level overscroll. Existing row pointer handlers remain intact, so ordinary taps, long-press reorder, and menu clicks retain their prior paths.

The indicator is intentionally small and occupies the list's first slot, using the existing muted text color. It rotates only during the active request, and reduced-motion preferences disable that animation. There is no new dependency, button, instruction copy, or other picker UI.

The test additions live beside the existing mobile server-list interaction tests. One dispatches touch events and confirms a qualifying pull emits once and prevents the browser's default movement; it checks both the active indicator and the absence of an idle indicator. Another begins at the menu and confirms movement cannot emit refresh. Existing tap and drag tests remain in the same suite.

## Approaches tried

I followed the current data flow rather than adding another network implementation or changing the on-open refresh behavior. The component emits a request and the parent invokes the established refresh function. This keeps tests for gesture behavior isolated from native fetch/network behavior and gives the UI an explicit promise-backed lifecycle.

I initially used `setProps()` on the mounted wrapper to simulate the parent toggling the optional `refreshing` prop. Vue Test Utils' inferred wrapper type rejected that prop in this suite, even though the component itself type-checked. The test now mounts a second instance with `refreshing: true` to assert the spinner state and checks the gesture instance remains idle. This retains coverage without weakening types or casting.

## Challenges and blockers

The build first caught that the test wrapper's inferred prop type did not expose `refreshing` through `setProps()`. Reworking the test to use a separately mounted active instance resolved this; the component build and tests passed afterwards. No device was available in this session, so the gesture has not been manually exercised in Android or iOS Capacitor webviews. The automated test validates the touch-event contract in jsdom, but cannot prove platform-specific touch arbitration. The normal list scroll and row menu paths are explicitly guarded in implementation and menu exclusion is tested.

The requested user guide check found no mention of refreshing in `user-docs/android-hub.md`; its current matching content covers tailnet discovery only. Therefore no doc wording was changed.

## Key learnings

Reachability refresh already has the correct completion boundary: the promise settles after all saved-server validations have returned, including their existing timeout behavior. The new feature therefore only needs to expose that promise to the list interaction and mirror its lifetime in UI state. In Vue Test Utils, mounting a stateful prop variant can be simpler and more strongly typed than mutating props on a wrapper whose inferred prop type is narrower.
